In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of elevated atmospheric CO2 on photosynthetic acclamation.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the photosynthetic acclamation to elevated CO2 is not due to limited nitrogen supply.

the effects of low nitrogen and elevated [CO2] on the acclimation of photosynthetic capacities in soybean are similar in that both reduce nitrogen as a percentage total leaf dry mass and decrease carboxylation capacity per unit leaf area, but that they are different in that the effects of elevated [CO2], but not low nitrogen supply, are to increase the ratio of RuBPC regeneration capacity to Vmax, and to decrease carboxylation capacities and Rubisco per unit nitrogen.
nitrogen supply does not appear to have a significant effect on the CO2 acclimative response in soybean.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
photosynthetic acclamation to elevated CO2 is not simply a response to limited N uptake, but that both elevated CO2 and N limitation have independent and additive effects.

elevated CO2 and nitrogen deficiency have similar effects on the allocation of nitrogen between structural and non-structural components of the plant, but the effects on the allocation within structural and non- structural components differ.

elevated CO2 and low nitrogen supply both decrease nitrogen as a percentage and as a concentration of leaf mass, and that both treatments also decrease photosynthetic capacity and Rubisco content, although the responses are opposite in direction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the photosynthetic capacity of plants grown at elevated CO 2 is not limited by the availability of nitrogen.
the effects of elevated [CO2] and nitrogen limitation are not the same, and that the effects of CO2 enrichment on photosynthesis cannot be attributed to nitrogen limitation.
plants do not necessarily need to reduce the expression or activity of their photosynthetic machinery to acclimate to elevated CO2.
